html:
Behavioral capabilities

Between the ages of 3 and 4, children see substantial gains in observable behavior across multiple domains. This one-year span often marks the transition from toddlerhood to early childhood, bringing new competencies in motor coordination, language use, social understanding, self-control, emotional management, memory, and problem-solving. A 2026 international study describes motor skills in early childhood (Figure) 88.

By age 4, children display significantly improved balance, strength, and coordination compared to age 3. Notably, a 4-year-old can hop on one foot and maintain one-foot balance for a few seconds, feats that a 3-year-old generally cannot perform 1. Four-year-olds also run and climb with greater agility; they can confidently walk up and down stairs one foot per step and ride a tricycle with better steering control 2. Running control shifts from simply moving fast to regulating pace and direction changes; you see quicker starts/stops and smoother forward-backward transitions 3. Four-year-olds can also catch a large ball (using the whole body) and walk on their tip toes 3. The study reports gross-motor percentile curves (Figure).

Fine motor control also advances between 3 and 4. Three-year-olds can scribble and stack a few blocks, but four-year-olds achieve new precision in hand-eye tasks. For example, a 4-year-old can cut paper with child-safe scissors, a skill uncommon at 3 1. Drawing and writing skills progress from basic shapes to more complex forms: a typical 3-year-old might draw a simple circle, whereas a 4-year-old can copy geometric shapes (like crosses or squares) and even draw a person with 2-4 body parts 1. They begin holding crayons or pencils with better control, allowing them to trace letters or write some characters by age 4 2. Such fine motor milestones (which also includes turning pages one at a time and unscrewing jar lids) illustrate the new dexterity and planning in hand movements that emerge during this period. Relatedly, 4-year-olds display a basic ability to categorize objects according to their functions 4, suggesting a emerging integration between semantic and motor systems. The study also measures fine-motor performance (Figure). A longitudinal study tracks motor development (Figure) 95.

Children’s language ability grows explosively between 3 and 4 years, in vocabulary, grammar, and communicative skills. Vocabulary size roughly doubles during this interval: the average expressive vocabulary expands from about 900-1,000 words at age 3 to roughly 1,500-1,600 words by age 4 5. This larger lexicon enables four-year-olds to express themselves on a wider range of topics. In addition to nouns and verbs, they regularly use adjectives and basic feeling words by age 4 (e.g. "long," "happy," "sad"), which are seldom heard from 3-year-olds 2. Sentence structure and grammar become substantially more complex; a 3-year-old typically speaks in telegraphic sentences of 3-4 words, but by 4 years children form longer sentences of  5-6 words or more 2. Four-year-olds reliably use grammatical markers that were just emerging at 3; for instance, they correctly use plurals, basic prepositions ("in," "on"), and present progressive "-ing" verbs 6. They also begin to grasp more complex grammar: by 4, most children understand basic past tense and can recite simple songs or nursery rhymes with correct phrasing 1. In fact, many 4-year-olds enjoy playing with language: they love poems or absurd phrases and can appreciate simple jokes (e.g. understanding the silliness of asking "Is that an elephant on your head?"). Furthermore, whereas strangers can catch only  75% of a 3-year-old’s speech on average, a 4-year-old’s speech is almost fully intelligible to unfamiliar adults 6. They also become more active conversationalists. Four-year-olds express ideas and feelings, not just labeling objects or needs 6. They can answer simple questions ("What do you do when you’re hungry?") and even start asking the endless "why" questions themselves as their curiosity blossoms 2. This ability to engage in back-and-forth dialogue and provide descriptions or narratives (for example, telling a brief story about their day) is a new capability that sets 4-year-olds apart from younger preschoolers. Overall, the transition from age 3 to 4 is marked by flourishing linguistic competence: more words, longer and grammatically richer sentences, and far more effective communication with others. A shared-reading study measures children’s oral language (Figure) 89. A preschool study examines narrative comprehension (Figure) 93.

Three-year-olds largely play side-by-side (parallel play) with minimal coordination, but by 4 years old children can begin truly playing together in cooperative and imaginative ways, marking a shift from simply being near other children to engaging with them toward shared goals 7. A 4-year-old is more likely to play games with rules with peers, negotiate roles in pretend play ("I’ll be the doctor, you be the patient"), and collaborate on a common project (building a fort of blocks together) than a 3-year-old. Along with this, sharing and turn-taking improve noticeably by age 4. Three-year-olds can take turns for short periods but often struggle with impulses to grab or hog toys. By 4, children better understand the concepts of "mine" versus "yours" and show emerging fairness; they are more willing to share and have learned basic turn-taking norms 2. Early friendships also form in this period. Although preschoolers’ friendships are still quite fluid, studies show that children of 3-4 can name particular peers as friends and maintain those preferences over a span of months. Four-year-olds often exhibit touching moments of empathy and loyalty in these friendships - for example, comforting a friend who is crying or declaring "I love my friend" - behaviors that are just beginning to appear at this age. By contrast, 3-year-olds are less consistent: they may play with others but are just as likely to abruptly say "You’re not my friend" over minor conflicts. The increased social stability and kindness at 4 reflect growth in understanding others’ feelings.

The fourth year also brings an expansion in imaginative play and the understanding of fantasy vs. reality. Around age 4, children’s pretend play scenarios become far more elaborate and story-driven; they enjoy inventing characters and narratives (playing house, pirates, superheroes, etc.) with peers or imaginary friends 2. Many 4-year-olds have imaginary companions and can engage in lengthy make-believe play, yet they typically can distinguish pretend from real by this age 2. This contrasts with 3-year-olds, who are only beginning to engage in simple pretend roles and may be more easily confused by fantasy. By 4, children also develop a sense of humor and trickery in social play. A common delight at this age is trying to fool others with playful deceptions (e.g. a child might giggle that they "tricked Mom into thinking I was asleep") 2. A 2026 play study tests false-belief reasoning (Figure) 91. The intervention study compares changes in false-belief performance (Figure).

The fact that a 4-year-old can intentionally deceive playfully (and also start to realize others might trick them) signals a new level of social cognition, reflecting a major cognitive-social milestone that typically occurs around 4 years: children begin to grasp that others have independent thoughts and can hold false beliefs (basic "theory of mind"); decades of developmental research using "false-belief" tests (like the classic Sally-Anne task) show a sharp transition in this age range. In one meta-analysis, the vast majority of 3-year-olds could not ascribe a false belief to someone else, whereas 4-year-olds reliably succeeded 8. In other words, a 3-year-old assumes everyone knows what they know, but a 4-year-old can begin to appreciate that another person might be unaware of certain facts or might be fooled by a situation. For example, at 3 a child will insist that a friend looking for a toy will check where the child knows the toy really is, even if the friend didn’t see it moved. By 4, the child is more likely to anticipate that the friend will have a false belief and look in the toy’s original location. This emerging theory of mind also manifests in everyday interactions: four-year-olds start lying or bluffing in simple ways.

The preschool years are a time of rapid growth in executive functions, with many executive abilities that are fragile or absent at 3 becoming reliably present by age 4. Four-year-olds exhibit much better impulse control compared to three-year-olds, showing signs of successful performance on both simple (i.e., pure response inhibition) and complex inhibition tasks (i.e., response inhibition plus alternative response) 9. For example, in the "Simon Says"-type Bear/Dragon game (where children must only follow commands given by a "nice bear" puppet and ignore a "naughty dragon" puppet), young 3-year-olds understand the rule but cannot resist mimicking the dragon’s commands. In contrast, most 4-year-olds can inhibit their impulses and successfully "freeze" for the dragon 10. Likewise, parents often notice that by age 4, children can handle simple instructions like "don’t touch that yet" or can wait a short time for a treat, skills that were very hard at 2-3.

Around age 4, children achieve a milestone in mental flexibility (the ability to shift to a new rule or perspective). A classic test is the Dimensional Change Card Sort (DCCS). A 3-year-old can sort cards by an initial rule (say, by color), but when the rule changes (sort by shape), the child perseverates (they keep sorting by the old rule even though they know it changed). By contrast, 4-year-olds can switch to the new rule and sort correctly after a rule change 11; researchers characterize this 3-to-4-year shift from perseveration to flexibility as a fundamental cognitive development 12. This newfound flexibility at 4 allows children to handle multi-step routines and adjust when rules or expectations change (for example, a 4-year-old can learn that at school they must line up quietly after playtime, even if at home playtime has no such rule, whereas a 3-year-old has difficulty with such context shifting).

Working memory capacity and the ability to follow complex directions also improve by age 4. A three-year-old can hold in mind and follow about two simple related commands in sequence, but by 4 years children can handle 2-3 step instructions reliably (especially if the steps relate to familiar contexts) 2. For instance, a 4-year-old can understand: "Close the book and give it to Mommy" or "Go to your room, find your shoes, and bring them here," whereas a 3-year-old might forget one of those steps or get confused after the first action; one study showed that when tasked with recalling and executing a sequence of actions (opening a series of drawers in the correct order to retrieve prizes), 3-year-olds could successfully remember two-step sequences, whereas 4-year-olds managed three- and four-step sequences reliably 13. This reflects both better attention span and memory. Educators note that four-year-olds can sustain attention on a single activity for longer periods than toddlers (often engaging in a task for 10+ minutes 14) and can shift focus under adult guidance without melting down. A longitudinal study models motor and executive-function development (Figure) 92. The researchers estimate changes over three assessments (Figure).

By 4 years, episodic memory shifts from mostly gist- (what happened) and script-based (basic steps) recall at 3 to more episodic, source- and context-tagged remembering. Four-year-olds recall personally experienced events with more of the "what-where-when" bound together (e.g. they can tell you not just that they went to the lab but which room particular activities happened in) and they outperform younger preschoolers on memory for the locations of events and on conjunctions between event content and place, although performance is still far from adultlike 15. Temporal information becomes more recoverable: across early childhood, memory for the order of past events shows pronounced gains, with preschoolers around four beginning to succeed on temporal-order tasks that would most three-year-olds 16, 17. Source monitoring also improves: by four, children are better able than three-year-olds to report where they learned something, though "source amnesia" errors remain common relative to older children 18. This richer episodic recall co-develops with more coherent autobiographical narratives; four-year-olds include more relational details and evaluative commentary than three-year-olds, consistent with sociocultural accounts of autobiographical memory emerging across the preschool years 19, 20. Four-year-olds also begin to pass tasks tapping episodic future thinking (projecting themselves into a specific future event), a capacity that typically emerges between ages 3 and 4 and reflects more explicit, self-referential episodic representations 21.

Development of episodic and autobiographical memory: The importance of remembering forgetting

Spatial reasoning also shows a clear inflection. One study involving classic mental-rotation puzzles with 2D "ghost" figures showed that the proportion of children performing above chance rises steeply from 3-4 years; only about 10% of 3-year-olds perform above chance while 40% of 4-year-olds do 23. Reorientation also improves qualitatively: whereas 3-year-olds search essentially at random in a rectangular layout, 4-year-olds begin to encode and use the room’s geometry to find hidden targets, although their feature/landmark use is still fragile and error-prone 24. In larger rooms after disorientation, 4-year-olds reliably use geometry but typically fail to exploit a salient landmark unless given brief spatial wording 25. They are also on the cusp of Level-2 visual perspective-taking: with simple scenes some 4-year-olds can reason about how an array looks from another viewpoint, but with multi-object arrays they still default to egocentric choices far more than older children 26, 27. Finally, gains in spatial language and construction play scaffold these abilities: richer command of relational terms (e.g., in front/behind/between) correlates prospectively with better number skills, and puzzle/block play between ages 2-4 predicts stronger spatial transformation performance by  4.5 years 28, 29.

Causal reasoning gets more principled: children start relying less on mere co-occurrence and more on temporal order, probabilities, and hidden mechanism. In temporal-priority tasks, far more four-year-olds than three-year-olds pick the earlier event as the cause; in one study, 41/50 four-year-olds performed perfectly across four trials versus 22/50 three-year-olds 30. Their inferences also incorporate abstract rules 31: in certain experiments, they can recognize basic rules 31 and resolve ambiguity by considering how likely each (usually implicit) explanation is, something three-year-olds struggle with 32, 31. This shift shows that by four, children are not only noticing patterns but also weighing probabilities when deciding what caused what, an ability that researchers see in simple ’blicket detector’ tasks where kids must infer which objects activate a machine 32. They also begin to link causal powers to hidden mechanisms: four-year-olds infer that an object’s internal parts explain its efficacy and track that causal property when parts move between objects, whereas three-year-olds more often lean on surface appearance 33. Four-year-olds more also selectively seek and remember satisfying "why" answers than younger peers 34, 35, supporting their own causal inductions. Finally, nascent counterfactual reasoning emerges in some basic tasks by four 36, 37, though it remains highly fragile and task-dependent 38, 39. These causal feats do, however, remain confined to the most basic systems and still appear to be subserved by fast, largely automatic processing (System 1) rather than fully reflective, System 2 reasoning, which comes online in forthcoming years 39.

Training data and optimization

In the 3-4 year window, the brain continues to pursue a handful of coupled optimization problems, each having a characteristic stream of "training data" and error routing that drives the aforementioned behavioral gains. The motor system keeps optimizing the same objective laid out for 2-3 (accurate terminal states with comfortable biomechanics under an energy/vigor budget) but the weights further tilt towards precision as opposed to adding new basic skills; efficiency rises, brute-force corrections drop, and vigor is better scheduled. Practically, this looks like a tighter feedforward controller trained by denser, more precisely timed errors. Cerebellar climbing-fiber teaching spikes remain the vector-valued supervisor calibrating forward/inverse models, now clearly necessary for learning to natural stimuli 40 and capable of grading step size via complex-spike dynamics; that supervision reduces endpoint variance, anticipates load, and improves anticipatory postural adjustments as tasks get faster and more coordinated. In parallel, basal ganglia keep converting practice into policy: distributional dopamine encodes multiple "expectiles" of return, letting the actor learn risk-sensitive action timing and effort allocation so movements become quicker yet smoother with fewer submovements. Corticospinal bandwidth is rising rapidly with early-childhood myelination (especially along the corticospinal tract 41) so distal control and bimanual coordination can be decomposed more finely, and cortical predictive controllers can pre-shape hand orientation earlier in the reach. Fine-motor trajectories reflect this optimization: grip aperture scaling and pre-shaping become more anticipatory, and everyday pointing/aiming begins to follow cleaner speed-accuracy tradeoffs 42. Offline, preschool naps consolidate: spindles upregulated by learning enhance retention 43, helping compile practiced subroutines into smoother, chunked skills. A 2026 trial examines cognitively enriched physical play (Figure) 94. The trial also reports memory measures (Figure).

The linguistic system is optimizing four coupled objectives: mapping new forms to meanings, compressing grammar into predictive rules, stabilizing an efficient speech motor code, and using pragmatics to choose informative utterances. Lexical growth (especially verbs) leans on cross-situational statistics 44 and syntactic bootstrapping 45: children track co-occurrence structure across episodes 44 and use context clues (especially the grammatical frame of the sentence (who is doing what to whom)) to narrow a novel verb’s meaning, so prediction errors in word-scene mappings and mismatches between syntax and event structure drive belief updates that yield faster, more accurate verb use 46. Grammar advances because the learner increasingly prefers rules that best predict the input; overregularization is the signature of that generalization pressure (e.g using "mouses" instead of "mice") 47, while caregiver recasts supply tightly time-locked contrastive feedback that reduces future surprisal for the same message 48. Behaviorally this shows up as Brown-stage IV-V morphemes (articles, regular past, third-person -s, copula/aux "be") entering spontaneous speech 49. In comprehension, children begin to anticipate upcoming words; processing difficulty tracks probabilistic prediction error (surprisal) 50, and better producers predict more 51, feeding a virtuous cycle between production and comprehension. Production itself is tuned by auditory-somatosensory error: controllers compare expected with heard speech and adapt articulatory commands 52; altered-feedback studies show robust, error-driven adaptation in young children 53, aligning with the observed jump in intelligibility and longer, morphologically richer utterances.

Social learning is dominated by three coupled objectives: predicting minds, internalizing norms, and becoming an informative, cooperative partner. For mind‐prediction, children prioritize learning how desires, beliefs, and especially knowledge access ("seeing leads to knowing") drive others’ actions; errors arise whenever behavior contradicts their current model (e.g a listener acts confused or a partner chooses unexpectedly) and these social prediction errors, plus caregivers’ frequent mental-state talk 54, update belief attributions and yield the observed jump in mental-state vocabulary and success on early ToM tasks 55. For norm acquisition, pedagogy and play supply dense, labeled data 56: demonstrations flag that an action is conventional, children then "overimitate" even causally irrelevant steps 57, 58, and third-party norm violations elicit protest; these tightly time-locked signals train a normative policy that shows up behaviorally as rule-following in games and explicit corrections of others 59. For cooperative pragmatics, the objective is to choose utterances that uniquely identify referents and maintain common ground; when messages are ambiguous, peers’ clarification requests function as error signals that drive rapid adjustments in referential specificity and repair skill across trials, producing more informative, partner-sensitive talk by age four 60, 61. Finally, prosocial choice is tuned by reputational and fairness feedback: children increasingly weight others’ helpfulness and simple equity rules when sharing 62, so approval, gratitude, and allocation outcomes reinforce selective generosity and early inequality aversion (which is quite unreliable at this stage 63). A preschool study examines learning through exploration (Figure) 90. The study compares exploratory behavior (Figure).

The episodic system is optimizing three coupled objectives: segmenting continuous experience into discrete events, binding those events’ elements into a detailed and retrievable "what-where-when" code, and imposing temporal order that supports coherent retelling and planning. Training data arrive as prediction errors at event boundaries: when the next state in a viewed or enacted sequence deviates from the child’s event model, boundary-linked surprise sharpens the model and boosts encoding, a mechanism formalized in Event Segmentation Theory and shown to enhance later recall at boundaries 64, 65. Hippocampal maturation and connectivity then translate these boundary-tagged signals into stronger bindings: across early childhood, better episodic recall covaries with hippocampal structure/function, and preschoolers’ performance on naturalistic what-where-when searches improves over this window 66, 67, 68. Errors in temporal and source attributions during retrieval (e.g., telling events out of order or misremembering "who told me") generate corrective feedback from adults and tasks. Caregiver elaborative reminiscing provides densely labeled supervision (wh-questions, confirmations, recasts) that fills gaps and tunes narrative structure, producing richer, more temporally organized autobiographical reports 69, 70.

Everyday life trains executive control through three practical objectives: executing multi-step scripts under distraction (morning routines, clean-up, "get your shoes then your jacket"), inhibiting prepotent responses to meet rules ("wait your turn," "don’t touch the stove"), and flexibly switching goals and roles across activities (ending play to eat; shifting from "doctor" to "patient" in pretend). Naturalistic errors are dense and well-timed: missed steps, spills, or social corrections act as salient feedback, and adult scaffolding (prompting, modeling, graded hints) tightens children’s working-memory maintenance and response inhibition, yielding fewer prompts needed, smoother transitions, and better compliance across weeks 9, 71. Self-generated "private speech" becomes a key control signal: children label steps aloud ("first socks, then shoes"), which reduces off-task behavior and frustration by converting language into top-down guidance 72. Mechanistically, everyday successes and slip-ups gate what is held vs. updated in working memory via basal-ganglia-PFC loops 73, while conflict and anticipated payoffs tune how much control to deploy ("expected value of control" in dACC 74), so routines progressively compress into chunked scripts with faster, more reliable initiation. Practice matters: repeated rule-governed play, movement classes, and classroom routines deliver the kind of structured, incremental demands that measurably strengthen preschool executive function 75. Social pretend play adds powerful set-shifting and perspective-keeping pressure, improving flexibility in natural dialogue and cooperative tasks 76. Finally, sleep stabilizes the day’s control policies (naps and good nighttime sleep enhance attention and emotion regulation the next day 77) so children arrive at four with longer on-task stretches, quicker regrouping after errors, and more adaptive switching. This recent study illustrates figure 3 Children’s Spatial Positioning Varied According to the Others’ Position in the Room (Figure).

Spatial learning in the wild pursues four everyday objectives: making stable structures, transforming shapes mentally, navigating to goals, and mapping symbols to real space; each objective delivers dense error that sharpens the system. Block and track building optimize "stability under load" and "fit/alignment": sagging bridges, topples, and mis-joins generate salient physical mismatches that drive revisions to part-whole geometry and support the jump from stacks to bridged spans and simple enclosures; the same assembly practice is predictive of later spatial and even math skill, indicating that these error streams translate into generalizable spatial programs 78, 79. Puzzle play optimizes "shape-pose correspondence": every piece is a supervised trial where non-fit and rotated-fit act as labeled negatives/positives, and the frequency and quality of puzzle play in the 2-4 window predict children’s spatial-transformation performance months later 80, 23; the need for effective tool use further incentivizes mental rotation. Wayfinding in homes, classrooms, and playgrounds optimizes "place finding under disorientation" and incentivizes cognitive map formation: wrong-door searches and detours supply navigation prediction errors; at this age children can reorient by the extended geometry of rooms but still struggle to use the geometry of freestanding objects, so boundary-based cues yield more reliable success than isolated beacons 81. Throughout, caregiver spatial talk and gesture ("under the bridge," "rotate it," "left of the red door") act like high-information recasts: they focus attention on diagnostic relations and reduce future surprisal in similar scenes, and longitudinal data show that richer spatial language in this period predicts children’s later spatial performance 82.

Neural development

During this window, the brain is still "overprovisioned" while continuing its long shift toward faster, cheaper, and more selective computation. At the cellular-mesoscale, association cortex is at or just past its maximum synaptic density; classic quantitative work places a prefrontal crest roughly around 3-3.5 years before protracted pruning begins 83, which is consistent with the well-described childhood hypermetabolic plateau where cortical glucose use approaches roughly twice adult levels near age four 84. This combination (dense circuit substrate plus high energy availability) lets the system explore large hypothesis spaces while it starts to tighten control.

Apparent "cortical thinning" is now visible on MRI across much of the mantle, not because tissue is vanishing but because intracortical myelin is increasing and redundant synapses are slowly being removed. Longitudinal early-childhood imaging shows thickness/volume rising rapidly in year one, flattening by year two, then trending downward into the preschool years 85; quantitative MRI and biophysical analyses tie this specifically to myelin accumulation within the cortical ribbon rather than degeneration 86. Functionally, those microstructural changes continue to shorten local integration windows and reduce the energy per transmitted bit, shifting dynamics from diffuse local coupling toward gated, policy-stabilizing interactions.

White-matter bandwidth continues its steep, tract-specific gains. Diffusion MRI across birth->6 years shows rising fractional anisotropy with falling radial diffusivity in major association bundles, including dorsal perisylvian language pathways (arcuate) and lateral frontoparietal segments (SLF II/III), which are measurably maturing across the preschool window 87. This means longer effective communication radius at roughly fixed power, enabling faster top-down selection and tighter perception-action coupling.
